book.title: The Role of the Ahî Organization

pages.title: What Was the Ahî Organization?
pages.content:
The Ahî Organization was a religious, social, and trade group. It started in Anatolia in the 13th century and played a big role in the founding of the Ottoman Empire. This group had a big effect on many areas of life, from work life to personal life. For a long time, it guided society and shaped a person’s moral and daily life. In workshops, this group organized work life for apprentices, experienced workers, and masters. As a trade group, it checked the quality of goods, set prices, and solved business problems.

A person’s character was very important in this group. Members had to be honest, generous, and thankful. They always encouraged good behavior, helped people in need, and stayed away from actions forbidden by the Qur’an and the teachings of the Prophet. For example, they did not drink alcohol or tell lies. With the help of role models, members learned good manners for daily life, such as walking on the street or visiting sick people.

pages.title: Training and Culture
pages.content:
Also, the group had a big effect on the cultural life of Anatolia, not just personal life. Young people started as apprentices and went through different levels until they became masters. But their training was not just about learning a job. Members also learned from wise teachers and experts. In their culture, not learning a job correctly brought shame in this world and after death. So, training to learn a job was very important, and people did not start a business before they were ready.

Like madrasas and dervish schools, Ahî organizations worked as important schools for the people in Anatolia. They were important cultural centers where people learned a job and how to be a good person. This helped Anatolian Turkish culture grow.

There are many stories about how Ahî organizations worked and how they trained apprentices. In fact, some words from these stories became Turkish sayings. Here are two of them:

pages.title: The Shoe on the Roof
pages.content:
The Ahî Organization helped workers and checked their work. They wanted every shop owner to do honest and quality work.

In a small town, a shoemaker wanted to make more money, so he began using cheap leather. Soon, his customers saw a problem. Their new shoes broke after only a few weeks. They became angry and went to the Ahî leader to complain.

The leader walked into the shop and looked closely at the poor-quality shoes. He decided to do something about it. He threw the low-quality shoes onto the roof of the shop. This was a big warning for every shop owner in town. It showed that the shoemaker did a poor job. If he did not improve the quality, he could not sell shoes in that town again. This is where the saying ‘pabucu dama atılmak’ comes from.

pages.title: The Secret of the Glass
pages.content:
In the past, in a town in Central Anatolia, a young apprentice wanted to open his own shop. However, in the Ahî tradition, an apprentice needed a special certificate from his master first. The young glassmaker asked for this certificate. But his master shook his head and said, “You are not ready yet.”

The apprentice did not listen to his master. He packed his things, went to another city, and opened a new shop. But things went wrong. All of his new glass cups and figures cracked after a short time. No one wanted to buy his work. He lost all his money and had to return to his master. He said, “I am sorry,” and his kind master forgave him.

They worked together for some more time. After that, the master looked at him and said, “Now you are ready.” He took the apprentice into a special dark room. Masters used this room to cool down hot glass slowly so it did not crack. Also, it was very easy to see mistakes in the dark.

Inside the room, a little sunlight came through a small hole in the ceiling. The master held up a hot piece of glass to the light. There was a tiny air bubble inside it. The master blew on it softly. “Püf!” The bubble disappeared.

At that moment, the apprentice understood his mistake. He also understood why his master had said, “You are not ready yet.” The glass pieces he had made before had cracked because he had not blown out those tiny air bubbles. He finally learned this important secret, thanked his master, and started a very successful business. In Turkish, the key point of a job is called ‘püf noktası.’

exercises.explanation: Use “had to” for a rule in the past, “to + verb” for a reason, and “not … yet” for “not now”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Had, to, yet.
feedback.incorrect: Check had to, to + verb and not … yet.

exercises.title: Practise: Correct the Sentences
exercises.instructions: Find the mistake and choose the correct form.
exercises.question: Which form is correct?

errorItems.sentence: The shoes breaked after a few weeks.
The apprentice not listened to his master.

exercises.explanation: Break → broke, forgive → forgave. Use “did not + base verb” for the past negative.

feedback.correct: Correct. Broke, did not listen, forgave.
feedback.incorrect: Check the irregular verbs and the negative.

exercises.title: Use: A New Context
exercises.instructions: Read about a baker today. Fill each gap from the word bank.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a new text?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Mr. Kaya is a baker. He was an [blank] for five years. Now he is a [blank]. He uses good flour, so his bread is [blank] work. His [blank] are very happy.
exercises.explanation: Apprentice, master, quality work and customers come from the book. Here they describe a baker today.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s words in a new text.
feedback.incorrect: Read the words around each gap.

exercises.title: Use: Check a Short Text
exercises.instructions: A student wrote about a shop. Find each mistake.
exercises.question: What should the student change?

errorItems.sentence: The shop owner have to be honest.
Yesterday, the customers goes to the shop.
The bread was bad, because the customers complained.

exercises.explanation: Use “has to” after he or she, a past verb with yesterday, and “so” for a result.

feedback.correct: Correct. Has, went, so.
feedback.incorrect: Check the verb forms and the linking word.

exercises.title: Use: A Good Worker Today
exercises.instructions: Write four to five sentences about a good worker you know.
exercises.question: What does this person do well?
exercises.explanation: Example: “My aunt is a tailor. She learned the job from an old master in our town. She was an apprentice for many years. She always uses good cloth and never lies about prices. She is a good worker because she is honest and careful.”

feedback.correct: Check: the job, how the person learned it, and because.

discussionPrompts.question: Say who the person is and what the job is.
Say how the person learned the job.
Say why the person is a good worker, with because.
discussionPrompts.example: He / She is a good worker because …

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Bring the whole book together in the Final Challenge.

exercises.title: Where and When
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: Where did the Ahî Organization start?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “It started in Anatolia in the 13th century …”

feedback.correct: Correct. In Anatolia.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of the book.

exercises.title: Words and Meanings
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning.
exercises.question: What do the words mean?

matchingPairs.right: a young person learning a job
a person with great skill in a job
a person who buys things from a shop
an official paper that shows you can do something

correctAnswer.apprentice: a young person learning a job
correctAnswer.master: a person with great skill in a job
correctAnswer.customer: a person who buys things from a shop
correctAnswer.certificate: an official paper that shows you can do something

exercises.explanation: These words are important in all four chapters.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each word matches its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Think about the stories in Chapters 3 and 4.

exercises.title: Members
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one word.
exercises.question: What did members have to be?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Members had to be honest, generous, and [blank].
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Members had to be honest, generous, and thankful.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Thankful.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: Like Schools
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: What were Ahî organizations like?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Like madrasas and dervish schools, Ahî organizations worked as important schools for the people in Anatolia.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Like madrasas and dervish schools.
feedback.incorrect: Find the word schools in Chapter 2.

exercises.title: Two Stories
exercises.instructions: Match each person with what he did.
exercises.question: Who did what?

matchingPairs.right: threw the shoes onto the roof
opened a shop in another city

correctAnswer.the Ahî leader: threw the shoes onto the roof
correctAnswer.the apprentice: opened a shop in another city

exercises.explanation: Chapters 3 and 4 tell two stories about Ahî workers.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each person matches his action.
feedback.incorrect: Look in Chapters 3 and 4.

exercises.title: The New Shop
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The apprentice’s new shop in another city was very successful.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “But things went wrong. All of his new glass cups and figures cracked after a short time. No one wanted to buy his work.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Things went wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 4.

exercises.title: Forgiving
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The master forgave the apprentice when he came back.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “He said, ‘I am sorry,’ and his kind master forgave him.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The master forgave him.
feedback.incorrect: Find the word forgave in Chapter 4.

exercises.title: A Saying
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 4 with two Turkish words.
exercises.question: What is the key point of a job called in Turkish?
exercises.fillBlanksText: In Turkish, the key point of a job is called ‘[blank].’
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “In Turkish, the key point of a job is called ‘püf noktası.’”

feedback.correct: Correct. Püf noktası.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of the book.

exercises.title: Shoes That Broke
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: When did the new shoes break?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Their new shoes broke after only a few weeks.”

feedback.correct: Correct. After only a few weeks.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 3.

exercises.title: The Secret of the Glass
exercises.instructions: Put the events in order.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: The apprentice asked for a certificate.
The apprentice opened a shop in another city.
The apprentice’s glass cracked and he lost his money.
The apprentice returned to his master.
The master showed him the secret of the glass.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 tells the story from the request to the secret.

feedback.correct: Correct. From the request to the secret.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Chapter 4 from the start.
